utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. I hope that everybody has been re-energised for the proceedings to come. There are several matters I'd like to deal with before we begin hearing the witness's evidence. The Chamber will first issue its oral ruling on Tomislav Kovac's request for assignment of counsel for the purposes of his testimony in this case filed on the record on 23rd of October, 2013. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution indicated via e-mail that it did not wish to respond to this request and that the accused filed a submission in support thereof on the 28th of October, 2013. The Chamber has considered Article 5 of the directive on the assignment of counsel, which provides for the assignment of counsel to three categories of individuals: Suspects, accused persons, and any person detained under the authority of the Tribunal. Although Kovac does not fall under any of these three categories at the moment, given that he was interviewed by the Prosecution as a suspect on several occasions between 2003 and 2010, and that he was assigned counsel for the purpose of his testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case in 2012, the Chamber orders the Registrar, on an exceptional basis, to assign counsel to Mr. Kovac and allows counsel to be present in the courtroom during his testimony. The Chamber will now turn to the Prosecution motion to exclude in part evidence of Tomislav Kovac filed on the 21st of October, 2013, as well as the Prosecution's motion for leave to reply to the accused's response thereto filed on the 28th of October, 2013. The Prosecution requests that paragraphs 7, 12 through 15, 19 and 20 of the statement of Tomislav Kovac be excluded as they are not relevant to the charges in the indictment. The accused in his response, filed on 28 October 2013, opposes the motion on the grounds that the Prosecution was allowed to elicit evidence on historical matters. Also, on the 28th of October, the accused circulated a revised version of Kovac's statement. Having reviewed the submissions and the statement, the Chamber is of the view that paragraphs 7, 12, 14, 15, 19, and 20 should be excluded as they pertain to issues not relevant to the indictment. However, the Chamber is of the view that paragraph 13, as it appears in the revised statement, may remain as it is at least of some relevance to the time frame of the indictment. The Chamber therefore grants the motion in part, orders the exclusion of paragraphs 7, 12, 14, 15, 19 and 20, allows the accused to tender the remainder of Kovac's statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and denies the Prosecution's request for leave to reply. The Chamber will now issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution motion to amend Exhibits P4771 and P7 -- strike it, P4772, filed on the 25th of September, 2013. In the motion, the Prosecution seeks to amend the expert report of Witness Dusan Janc admitted under seal as P4771, as well as the public redacted version admitted as P4772, by replacing charts included in the report with revised versions. The Prosecution submits that it discussed the issue with the Defence on the 18th of September, 2013, and that the Defence does not object to the replacement of the charts. The Trial Chamber has reviewed the revised charts and in accordance with its ruling of the 6th of March, 2012, concerning the expert report of witness Dusan -- I'm sorry, Dean Manning, the Chamber is satisfied that the revised charts shall replace the old versions and instructs the Prosecution to upload them into e-court as such. Next in relation to the accused's motion to admit documents previously marked for identification, before a ruling on that motion, the Chamber would like to inquire with the Prosecution regarding its submission on the documents marked for identification as D2518. I forgot the -- to mention the date of filing of the motion but it was on the 5th of September, 2013. The Chamber notes the Prosecution's response to the accused's motion on 13th of September, 2013, wherein in objects to the admission of MFI D2518 based on concerns of authenticity given that the original document in B/C/S is not available. At this stage, the Chamber would like to receive further submissions from the Prosecution as to its reasons for being concerned about the authenticity of this document. For the remainder of matters, I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any matters to be discussed? Then we will bring in the witness. Yes, good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May I, before we start, then, just introduce Ms. Ellen Naughton who was been with my team since June of this year. She is a graduate of Bond University in Australia with a bachelor of laws and bachelor of international relations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Zametica, before you commence your evidence, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal, that is Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony, compelled under such circumstances, could not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence, save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning, my learned friends. Good morning, everyone. I'm glad that we are in good form, all of us, after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Zametica.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, I know that you understand both languages but here we -- every word of Mr. Karadzic should be translated so could you put a pause between the question and answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- which is very imperative here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As your testimony will be live, I will try to ask you some relevant questions in the briefest form possible, as the answers to those questions could help us to understand the situation and what you had the opportunity to witness and see personally. Can you tell us, briefly, your first and last name, your father's name, when and where you were born, and everything else that you consider important about your background.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I was born in Banja Luka, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1955. The name of my father was Muris. He was a Muslim. My mother, Olga, was of mixed Slovak-German descent. Although I was born in Banja Luka, I didn't live there very long. My mother divorced my father when I was still a baby, and my mother, of course, took me with her when she returned to the place where she came from, which is a Slovak village north of Belgrade in the -- what was then known as the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina. I was given the name Omer, I shall spell that out, O-m-e-r, which was a Muslim name. Just like Francois is recognisably a French name or Helmut is recognisably a German name, Muslim name Omer was recognisably very Muslim and that was the name I was given at my birth. But I grew up in this Slovak village called Padina and my mother tongue was Slovak. It was not Serbian or Serbo-Croat as it was then known. I grew up in a house where Slovak and German were spoken. My mother and grandmother conversed exclusively in German. And I went to elementary school, a Slovak elementary school, so I grew up actually among Slovaks, who were a national minority in Yugoslavia living among many other national minorities in that province of Vojvodina. Subsequently, my mother's career took her to Belgrade and I continued my elementary education in Belgrade where, of course, I had to learn this new language called the Serbo-Croat language. But we only stayed in Belgrade, I think, for three years because my mother's career then took her to Ljubljana, the capital of the then Socialist Republic Slovenia, and I had to learn yet another new language, this time Slovene, which is quite different from Serbo-Croat. And I continued my elementary education in Slovenia, started my secondary education there too. When I was 18, this was back in 1973, my mother and I moved to England for family reasons. My mother decided to remarry and she married someone who at the time worked and lived in London. So I had to learn yet another language, this time English. When I still lived in Yugoslavia I used to go and visit my father in Sarajevo, where he lived, quite frequently. So the -- what that meant was that I actually got to know Yugoslavia quite well, or perhaps better than your average Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. Could you now please also summarise for us the progression of your education, by just listing the degrees you were awarded, if you can?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I received my university, my higher education in England. I went to several English universities. I obtained a BA in modern history and politics. I obtained an MA in 20th century international history, and I also obtained a Ph.D. I specialised in -- in the area of the Cold War. I was very interested in the initial stages of the Cold War, and I did a Ph.D. on British strategic planning, on British military planning during the early stages of the Cold War, 1945-46-47. That was my main academic interest, and the Ph.D. had nothing to do with Yugoslavia. So I did something in mainstream British history or international history. In between my MA and my Ph.D., I -- I worked for a while at an English secondary school, I taught as a teacher, I taught modern British history and modern European history. And subsequent to that, I served during 1980-81 in the Yugoslav People's Army, as it was called. I did a stint in the infantry, as an infantryman. So this was the time just after Tito had died. But immediately after completing my military service, I returned to England to do my Ph.D., which I completed in 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that this answer also included everything that you held in terms of professional positions. Is there anything that you might add about that? Before coming into the midst of our crisis, what were the positions that you held? You worked in some institutes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: That's right. But before I started working at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London, which was, I think, back in 1990, I had a series of part-time jobs teaching international history, Cold War. I used to teach at, for example, I used to teach for the open university, I used to teach a course on nuclear weapons. I used to teach international history for the department of extramural studies at the University of Cambridge. I taught international history for a while at -- as a tutor, as an external tutor at Wadham College, Oxford. But those were not permanent appointments. The institute you referred to, the International Institute for Strategic Studies, offered me a post in 1990 at a time when Yugoslavia began to disintegrate, and they needed someone who was an expert on the Balkans. Strictly speaking, I was not an expert on the Balkans. I was an expert on the Cold War. And in fact, I had published on the Cold War, academic pieces, essays and articles, but I had also published an article on Yugoslavia for "The Times" newspaper and they noticed that. And as a result, they wanted to talk to me because they needed someone who was an expert on the Balkans. Those were few and far between at the time in the -- in the UK. So I was offered this job, and I took it. After I completed my stint at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, I worked as a research fellow at the Polytechnic of Central London, which subsequently became the University of Westminster. You may or may not know that all the polytechnics in the U.K. overnight became universities. So -- but that was my last appointment in the UK before I went to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go further, line 18 on previous page should read "International Institute for Strategic Studies." And, Dr. Zametica, you said a while ago that you did a stint in the JNA. Could you expand on it? Was it a compulsory on your part? And what was your nationality then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The JNA, the Jugoslovenska Narodna Armija, or the Yugoslav People's Army, the system in Yugoslavia at the time was that you had to -- if you were an able-bodied young man over 18 you had to do your stint in the military. There was an exception, however, and the exception pertained to those people who had residence abroad. So in my case, I didn't have to serve in the JNA because I had residence abroad. So it wasn't compulsory for me and it would not have been -- I would not have commited an illegal action had I not joined the army or agreed to go there. But in my case, you know, it was a personal decision. I believed that it was part of a man's education to do a stint in the army, and I thought, you know, a man's education is kind of incomplete if he doesn't have some military experience. So even though many people considered it a strange thing to do, for me to leave the UK and go to Yugoslavia to do a period in the army at a time when there was a great deal of speculation about the possibility of a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia following Tito's death, I thought that I should nevertheless do it, and I -- I don't regret doing it. So I hope I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it your nationality was then a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my -- as you know in Yugoslavia, you could declare yourself Serb, Croat, Slovene, whatever, but there was a special category which was allowed for those who considered themselves as Yugoslavs. And in the population censuses which took place when I was still living in Yugoslavia, I would always declare myself a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. Could you just tell us briefly what you knew and to what extent about our crisis in Yugoslavia, in the 1990s, before you came to Bosnia and joined the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: My job at the International Institute for Strategic Studies was to do -- was to prepare or write what they called an Adelphi paper. Adelphi papers were short studies about 90, 100 pages long, so we are talking about a booklet, which the institute publishes in relation to whatever current crises are going on in the world or important international issues that need to be addressed. Because Yugoslavia began to find itself in a crisis in the late 1990s -- late 1980s and the beginning of 1990s, that should be late 1980s, I was asked to prepare a paper on the Yugoslav crisis. So at the time I began my work there was still no war, but obviously I had to follow the situation very closely. I was subscribed to several newspapers from different parts of Yugoslavia. I went on several visits in Yugoslavia in order to do research for my paper. I met quite a few actors on the Yugoslav scene at the time, as well as journalists, diplomats, people like that. So, yes, I -- I had to very closely follow the situation, and be, as it were, at the cutting edge of the research on the subject. That was expected of me. So on a daily basis I followed events, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. Could you tell us whether you and I knew each other before this crisis, whether we had any kind of personal relationship? Actually, you can also tell us when we first met and how our cooperation evolved before you arrived.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: We certainly did not know each other before the crisis developed. The one person on the Bosnian Serb side that I knew well, at the beginning of the crisis, was the late Nikola Koljevic. I also met Biljana Plavsic on one of my visits to Yugoslavia, to Sarajevo. But I did not meet you, I believe, before sometime in 1992, and if I remember correctly, we first met in Villa Bosanka in Belgrade after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina had already begun, but we did have, I think, telephone conversations beforehand. So we knew each other on the telephone, and you probably gathered information about me from -- from Professor Koljevic, maybe also from Mrs. Plavsic, I don't know, but we did -- we certainly did not know each other before the crisis. And, well, I think I have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you come to Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, Republika Srpska, and what was the position that you came to? What was your role, what was your position, in the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I arrived in -- in Republika Srpska in, I think, October 1993. When I arrived I still had no position as such, and I was not given one until, I think, February 1994, when you appointed me your advisor. But my advisory role, as it were, concerned the area of international relations, which is where my expertise lay. In other words, communicating with the international community. I was your aide in matters concerning relations with international organisations, the diplomatic effort that Republika Srpska was making. Of course, in all this, my knowledge of the West and my knowledge of the English language presumably played a role in my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the whole, how were you received, by me, by the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Well, my problem in -- in Republika Srpska was my Muslim background. I say "my problem." I didn't have a problem with my Muslim background but I think some people did. Certainly, Professor Koljevic did not, and certainly you did not. But I think some others may have had such a problem, which is, I suppose, understandable. I think your -- your wife was suspicious of my background. I think your daughter, too, didn't like me because of my ethnic background. But you never exhibited any feelings that would indicate to me you had a problem with that. On the contrary, you -- you were very open about the fact that you knew my ethnic background but that was absolutely no problem for you. And I must say, had I -- had I felt that you in any way disliked me on account of my ethnicity, I would have left. I would not have felt comfortable. But I never felt uncomfortable with you because of that. I think some people in the army didn't like me because of it, or thought I was suspect because of it, but I didn't pay much attention to that. I felt very comfortable working with you. I should perhaps add that within your own family, your wife and your daughter, as I subsequently found out from you, had drawn to your attention the fact that I had a Muslim background and that perhaps I was not the right person to be appointed in the place where I was, but I think you fought against that and I must say this is to your credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the army and persons close to me. In addition to ethnic background, were there other reasons for suspicion, in terms of your British background?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, possibly. Sorry. [In English] Maybe so but I would not like to speculate on the subject. I really don't know what was being said behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But apart from that, on the whole, did you manage to get insight into what was going on? Were you part of brainstorming sessions, the process of decision making, especially in terms of contacts with foreigners, humanitarian issues and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Given the position I held in the Presidency, I was privy to a lot of information. I think I was privy to everything that was important. So you always shared with me information about the international scene that you had, information about the domestic scene, information about relationship with Milosevic, information concerning relationships -- relationship with the Army of Republika Srpska. So everything that was important and you knew about it, in principle I would also know about it. So, yes, I was -- I was privy to a lot of information. I must say I -- I did not read intelligence reports. There are two kinds of intelligence reports reaching Presidency, I think, on a daily basis: Military intelligence and state security intelligence. But you had your special advisors for those two sectors. I think they were General Subotic for military matters and Gordan Milinic for state security matters, so they would read those reports. Although I must say I didn't miss much, it would appear, in the sense that you would sometimes share or show me intelligence reports. And I remember one occasion when, I think it was in 1994, when you asked me to come to your office, you asked me to sit down and you handed me a report, and you asked me: "Read it, please, and tell me what you think about it." And so I started reading it and it was a military intelligence report signed by General Tolimir, who was the head of the Bosnian Serb military intelligence, and it was quite a long report. And when I finished reading it, you asked me: "Well, what do you think about it?" And I said: "President, I've never read so much rubbish in my life." And you laughed and said: "Yes, exactly. This is what they do. They just send me lies." And you said: "You know what I think General Tolimir does every morning? He gets up, drinks his coffee, reads his newspapers, then takes his scissors, starts cutting the newspapers, makes a collage, and then starts typing his military intelligence reports which he then sends to me. And I'm never again," you said, if I remember correctly, "I'm never again going to read the rubbish." And so this is where it ended. But I mention this episode just to illustrate the fact that what you were receiving from your own people, quote unquote, did not, it would appear, amount to very good intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. You were asked to appear in public from time to time and present the views of the leadership with regard to particular matters. Were there ever any misunderstandings? Did we ever have to issue denials of anything that you presented as our position? Or was everything always accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No. I cannot remember a single occasion when you or either anyone else from the leadership, civilian leadership or even military leadership of Republika Srpska ever denied anything I said in public. So I cannot remember a single such occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Chamber whether you became aware of my positions on war and peace? And to the best of your knowledge, what were these positions and what were they like?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: That's a rather large question you just put to me. I remember one occasion when we were talking to Mr. Yasushi Akashi, when you said to him -- and I cannot remember the exact date, but I do remember that you said to him: "Mr. Akashi, I'm not interested in cease-fires. I'm interested in a permanent peace settlement." And I quote this, these words of yours, in order to illustrate what essentially your approach was to the questions of war and peace. Of course, you, before talking about cease-fires or permanent peace settlement, there was a period when you had to -- when you were negotiating with the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats about a political settlement in the context when there was still peace, in other words before the hostilities broke out in -- in 1991 -- sorry, in 1992 in Bosnia. And of course, I was following all of this from my position in London at the International Institute for -- for Strategic Studies, and there were two particular episodes which stand out from that period. One is -- one is the attempt to reach a political settlement in Bosnia, an attempt associated with the name of Adil Zulfikarpasic. And the other episode that stands out is the so-called Cutileiro Peace Plan. Now, as far as I know, you did your best to reach a settlement with Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic, who -- who was co-founder of the Stranka Demokratske Akcije, the SDA, the Muslim party, to call it simply, the Muslim party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The other founder was, of course, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. But Mr. Zulfikarpasic, whom I knew personally before the war, Mr. Zulfikarpasic subsequently broke away from the SDA, which he helped found, and founded his own party called the MBO, the Muslimanska Bosnjacka Organizacija, but he will be remembered in history for his effort to -- to ensure peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina before -- before what he feared, war broke out. And in order to do that he went to Mr. Izetbegovic, asking him, you know, are you aware that we have -- this is summer of 91 -- are you aware, he asked him, that we are about to, you know, start fighting each other, with the Serbs and the Croats and so on? And according to Zulfikarpasic's account, Mr. Izetbegovic authorised him to go and negotiate with the Serb side about a possible -- about a possible deal, settlement, with the Serbs, within some kind of Yugoslavia. Although, of course, hostilities already had broken out in Yugoslavia on 25th of June, 1991, with Slovenia and Croatia declaring independence, but there was still, you know, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, and of course Bosnia-Herzegovina. And Mr. Zulfikarpasic thought he had Mr. Izetbegovic's backing for this so he approached you and your colleagues in the Bosnian Serb leadership, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, and according to his account, there was agreement between you. And he subsequently went to Belgrade to see Mr. Milosevic, who also agreed with the proposals, which amounted to some kind of rump Yugoslavia containing Bosnia-Herzegovina and possibly Croatia. But if Croatia didn't want it, it could secede. Now, the interesting thing about that particular peace initiative, as it were, was that it was the only one that did not propose a territorial division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you had agreed to it, according to Mr. Zulfikarpasic. Now, the whole thing, of course, came to nothing because subsequently Mr. Izetbegovic, according to Mr. Zulfikarpasic, turned around and didn't want to have anything to do with the settlement he initially approved of, and so the whole thing collapsed. But it was an interesting attempt to -- to reach peace, not just in Bosnia-Herzegovina but -- but in the rest of Yugoslavia, minus Slovenia possibly and Croatia, which went wrong. So that's why I mentioned this particular Zulfikarpasic initiative because I think it's kind of been forgotten and your own part in it has been forgotten. And it -- although, you know, it was -- it was probably going to be difficult to implement it or to completely agree on the package, it was still a better alternative than -- than war. But as I said, the whole thing collapsed, unfortunately. The other outstanding episode from the peace period, regarding initiatives to reach a settlement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course was the Cutileiro Plan which you also backed and which initially Mr. Izetbegovic also agreed to. I can't remember the exact dates, February 1992, March 1992. This is the period we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zametica, may I -- may I just try to save time? In relation to what you know about Zulfikarpasic, did you actually talk to him about that? Did you learn certain things from him in personal contacts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Mr. Zulfikarpasic and I mostly talked about antiquarian books because we shared a passion for collecting antiquarian books on the Balkans, written mostly in French, German, English, and we were in fact rivals up to a point as collectors. But his funds were infinitely greater than mine. Yes, we also talked about politics. But, no, regarding this particular matter, we didn't talk about. I met him several times, but prior to this particular initiative which took place, I think July-August 1991. Yeah, 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Since Ambassador Cutileiro testified, could I ask you to summarise for us what you saw for yourself, what my position was with regard to peace efforts, peace plans, in which the international community mediated? You took part in some of the decision-making, and you probably spoke about that, presenting our position to the public.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: After those two peacetime peace plans, which -- which -- well, it seems that I don't have enough time to talk about the Cutileiro Plan, but if you say that Ambassador Cutileiro has already been a witness here, that must have been already covered. So I'm not going to waste this Tribunal's time talking about that, especially because I was not personally involved. But regarding your question now, regarding the other peace plans, I think there were -- there were four more during the war, starting with the Vance-Owen Plan, followed by the Owen Stoltenberg Plan, followed by the Contact Group Plan, followed by in the -- in the end by the Dayton Peace Plan which is the conference, the -- that ended the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Looking at those four plans, I think from my own experience having been involved in most of them, your attitude was always to gain a political settlement within Bosnia and Herzegovina that would satisfy the Serb side, obviously, and I don't think there is a single plan that you -- of those four that you particularly objected to. I think in essence you accepted all of them. You accepted even the Vance-Owen Plan. I know that because even though the Bosnian Serbs as such rejected in the end the Vance-Owen Plan, you personally didn't. The Serbs did but not you. You accepted it. You informed the members of the Assembly of Republika Srpska at the session in, I think, Bijeljina before the final rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan, but did you -- that you actually wanted to accept it. This is what I heard from someone who was present then. And you had in fact signed the Vance-Owen Plan in Athens, if I remember correctly. I wasn't personally involved with that, but this is what I understand was the case. Certainly, you accepted the Owen Stoltenberg Plan. You also, in essence, accepted the Contact Group Plan. I mean, in the end it was rejected by the Bosnian Serbs, but the Contact Group Plan was really problematic in its semantics rather than in its essence. And I knew that you were personally in favour of it but couldn't really push it past the opposition from, you know, the -- the -- some -- some, I would say, vested interests on the Bosnian Serb side, maybe the -- some -- some members of the Assembly who did not like the territorial aspect of it. I don't think the constitution was the problem. And of course, you also accepted the Dayton Peace Plan. That may sound obvious but it isn't, really, because the delegation you sent to Dayton, and I was a member of that delegation, it was an eight-member delegation. In Dayton we, in fact, rejected the final peace plan. This may or may not be well known, I don't know. I don't think it's particularly well known in Republika Srpska or in Serbia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina for that matter. What happened on the last day in Dayton, on the 21st of November, 1995, was that Mr. Milosevic, who had pushed us aside, and so we hardly participated in the work of the Dayton conference, and of course Mr. Holbrooke, who was the main actor on the -- on behalf of the international community, if you like, or on behalf of the United States, the two are not the same, I should add, although very often they seem to be, Mr. Holbrooke was also quite happy to ignore us. So the delegation of Republika Srpska did not know until the last day what had actually been agreed. And on the last day, Mr. Milosevic came, accompanied by Mr. Bulatovic of Montenegro and by Mr. Milan Milutinovic, the Serbian Foreign Minister, and he showed us this map, and when Mr. Krajisnik, the leader of our delegation in Dayton, saw the map, he went red in the face, and told Mr. Milosevic that history and the Serbian people will never forgive you this. And we then, the members of the delegation of Republika Srpska, subsequently held a little session where each one of us had to declare himself, as it were, where he stood regarding the peace plan at Dayton, and we all said that we opposed it for this or that reason. And so we left Dayton without signing the Dayton Accords. Milosevic had Mr. Milutinovic sign it on our behalf, as it were, but the Bosnian Serbs did not accept the Dayton settlement. When we arrived in Belgrade, and we travelled in the same plane with Mr. Milosevic and his delegation, we dispersed, we were told that next day there would be some kind of big conference in Belgrade and we should hang around in Belgrade, but that night we were all arrested at different locations in Belgrade. When I say "arrested," I mean to say that we were all picked up by the police and sent to or driven to one of the most luxurious prisons in the world, the former villa of President Tito at Dobanovci, outside Belgrade. And so we were in this luxury arrest place but suddenly, you know, telephone lines went dead and we could not call anybody. And of course we were looking at each other significantly. Nothing needed to be said. We knew we were arrested. And we didn't really know whether to fear for our lives, we didn't know what was going on. I personally kicked up a fuss and demanded to be connected to Mr. Jovica Stanisic, the head of Serbian state security, whom I vaguely knew. This was initially refused, but then I insisted and I even began shouting at the personnel in the villa. So finally they did connect me to him by telephone and I said to Mr. Stanisic that I demanded to get out because I had not seen my wife for three weeks, and wanted to be rejoined with my wife. And he laughed and said: Look, I'm going to let you -- I'm going to let you out, but you must promise me that you will, the following morning, turn up at the villa because there is going to be this big meeting and we don't want anyone to be absent. So I did, and as soon as I got out, I got to a telephone and telephoned you, explaining to you what had happened. And I think - correct me if I'm wrong - I think I told you that, you know, your life may be in danger because we really didn't know what was going on. But by the tone of your voice, I -- I gathered -- we spoke in some kind of semi-coded language. By the tone of your voice I gathered that you had, in fact, made up your mind to accept the Dayton peace settlement, and in fact you did the following morning turn up at Dobanovci. We were there. It was kind of an all-Serb meeting, only the patriarch was missing, but everybody came. The president of Montenegro was there of course, all the -- Milosevic's ministers. Thankfully his wife was not there. But apart from her and the patriarch, everyone else was. And I remember Mr. Milosevic pushing you into some kind of small room at one stage and he probably offered you a fountain pen to sign a piece of paper. Correct me if I'm wrong. Anyway, to cut a long story short, you also accepted the Dayton peace plan at a -- at a -- in a situation where none of your -- none of the members of your delegation had in fact accepted. We had in fact rejected it. Whether that was clever or not on our part, I don't know. I have mixed feelings about that. But we did reject it and you did accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. The details are really interesting but I have to hurry up a little. You mentioned the opposition, the deputies, and the efforts that I had to make to achieve anything. However, an expert witness of the Prosecution we've heard here, Dr. Donia - for the parties, it's his expert report in my case - said, for instance, that the Assembly of Republika Srpska heard open debates and one could often hear critique addressed to Karadzic, Mladic and others. And despite that, I quote: "The Assembly unanimously, or with just a few votes against, passed and endorsed all the important measures proposed by the leadership. There was only brief debate about proposed measures." What is your view? Was it easy for me to deal with that Assembly consisting of 83 people's representatives? Was it all that simple for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before -- Mr. Zametica, yes. Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just if Dr. Karadzic could oblige us with the 65 ter number and the page reference for that quote, it would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately I'm not able to starts up my computer here so I can't tell you that. But that's the expert report of Dr. Robert Donia, the chapter on institutions, first institutions and then subheading: "The Assembly of Bosnian Serbs." It's at the beginning of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you can offer the reference to the Prosecution during the break. But in the meantime, shall we proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do I need to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No. There is no need for you to repeat the question. Whether you had it easy with 83 members of the Assembly, well, the short answer is no. Not at all. In fact, my impression about your place in the political universe called Republika Srpska was that even though you held the title of president, in my view you were a weak president, weak in the sense of your power did not extend very far. My -- my firm impression, and I have this impression to this -- I hold on to this view to this -- to this day, is that you had very little power in -- in Republika Srpska. I felt that there were other, more powerful factors than you. I felt that, for example, the Army of Republika Srpska was a power unto itself, pursuing its own policies, domestic as well as foreign policies, and being regularly insubordinate to you. I felt that you did not have the control over the police. I felt that you did not have the control over the Assembly members, even though they may have been the members of your own party. I felt that you did not have control over your own driver. I felt that you did not have control over your own wife. And I felt that you certainly didn't have control over your own daughter. So not that your daughter and your wife were necessarily political factors, but in the case of your daughter, she did prove to be something of a factor in relation to the international media. So I felt were you a weak president from that point of view. You had very little control over what was going on in that -- in that chaos called -- called Republika Srpska in the period 1992-95. I also felt that you did not have your own people in the government of Republika Srpska. Where you did have some kind of autonomy, that was in the field of foreign affairs, and this is where I felt happy working with you because I knew that you could take initiatives there, you could make some impact there, and this is what was important to me. The idea was to attain a political settlement that would be favourable and fair, and this is the area where -- where you actually did do a lot, but not elsewhere. So to go back to your original question, was it easy for you to deal with those 83 Assembly members, no, it wasn't, because they were all very individualistic. They all had their own local interests to defend. They very often were very arrogant. They -- you know, one might call them robust. But I don't know where Dr. Donia got his information from, but it's clearly wrong, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. Another expert witness, Mr. Treanor, Patrick Treanor, in his report before this Court, in the summary, paragraph 15, E15, wrote as follows: "The formal authorisations, the formal powers of the president in extraordinary situations were rather broad and included a considerable degree of control over security forces such as the army and the police, as well as the local regional authorities with the mediation of wartime Presidencies and commissioners. Thanks to the overwhelming majority of SDS deputies in the Assembly, the Presidency effectively had control over members of the government and, through the SDS, over local and regional authorities as well." How did you see my use of these powers in extraordinary situations? You mentioned a moment ago local authorities. How did you see the SDS party? Was it unanimous? Was it united? And how did you view my use of these constitutional powers that were indeed broad? And how did you see the relationship between central authorities and the local ones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: May I ask you whether, when you said Mr. Treanor, are you referring to Ian Traynor, the "Guardian" journalist?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. Patrick Treanor is an expert for political systems. He appeared as an expert witness here for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Treanor spelling, T-r-e-a-n-o-r.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. The local factors in Republika Srpska, that's -- that's a separate and very long story, but I would argue that -- and this is partly my experience and partly what other people told me, so partly what I saw with my own eyes and partly talking to other people, ministers or local officials. Local power in Republika Srpska was the only one that actually properly functioned. When -- when Bosnia and Herzegovina began disintegrate and when Republika Srpska began to be created, the only thing that actually functioned were the old local authorities. And the people there, on the Bosnian Serb side, as far as I could tell, were extremely powerful. They were local chieftains, local masters of life and death. They would be people who would run their municipalities and not ask many questions about -- they would not ask many questions from you or from Mr. Krajisnik and so on. They were -- they were very powerful people who decided on practically everything in their municipalities, and they -- they felt that they were the most important people in the world. They felt that if they -- if their municipality falls to the Muslims, this would be the end of Serbdom. I think you had very little power over these individuals, especially at the beginning of the war, when it was difficult to communicate and everything was in chaos. I would say that the local forces, as it were, in Republika Srpska, sometimes worked even against you. They always certainly defended their own narrow local interest. They didn't have the broader vision of the state. The state was still being created. And so we must see that in that particular context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. Were you aware of the powers held by municipalities under the previous socialist system and the degree of their autonomy, especially in the area of defence? Were you familiar with these vestiges of socialism and did they continue during the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No. I can't say that I have -- that I had -- I had expert knowledge about the pre-war municipalities' responsibilities, but of course, I -- I seem to remember that they had pretty wide powers, especially in terms of local defence. There was a system called Teritorijalna Odbrana in the old Yugoslavia, the Territorial Defence. So I imagine this continued when the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned the army. Were you aware to what extent I was involved in the operative and tactical levels of command over the army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I don't think you did anything of the kind. I mean, in terms of operative and tactical levels of command over the army, I think you -- you left that to the army itself. I think you had responsibilities with regard to -- to any strategic decisions, but with regard to the day-to-day operative and tactical levels, I do not think you -- you were particularly involved. My experience is that -- is that, you know, you and I talked mostly about the international situation and about the forthcoming peace conference and 90 per cent of the time we would discuss such matters, and I can't really remember you going on about, you know, the army should have done this or that. I'm not saying you were not interested but you certainly didn't -- didn't tell me anything about it. I cannot remember you as someone who -- who was on a daily basis concerned with what was going on in terms of a particular military operation. I remember it was, you know, a low intensity war and so there weren't many days when, you know, there was intense fighting somewhere. There was always some sniping, some shelling, some -- some fighting, but big operations were few and far between.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what my position was vis-à-vis this fighting and the lulls in fighting and the sniper activity and shelling? What were you able to observe as to my attitude to this belligerence and the developments on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: As I said, we never talked a great deal about such matters. I remember you saying that sniping on the Bosnian Serb side, sniping from the Bosnian Serbs was stupid, that it didn't get the Serbs any military advantage, and I think you were against it. The same regards irresponsible shelling or instances when there was some shelling and you had disapproved of it because you just thought it senseless or unnecessary. But we didn't really talk much about military matters. I think you were more concerned about -- about how to attain a political settlement, and this is what we talked about, rather than, you know, what is going on on the battlefields. This was not -- this was not something you and I talked a great deal about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an idea about the position held by Bosnian Serbs and myself on humanitarian issues, regarding civilians, especially those of the other two warring parties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll come back to this after the break. But Mr. Zametica, you just mentioned that Mr. Karadzic was against sniping and shelling on the ground that it would not be advantageous to the Serb side. In relation to that statement, could you tell us how you understood the snipings and shellings to be? What shellings and what snipings did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not referring to anything in particular. I was -- I was talking about sniping and shelling in general, as something disapproved of by Dr. Karadzic. I'm not sure that I understand your question, when you ask me what snipings did I talk about? Did you ask me about anything in particular? Or any particular event or did you -- did you mean to ask me, you know, what was Mr. Karadzic's general position on the subject?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will quote what you said. It's from line 13. It's in answer to Mr. Karadzic's question: "I remember you saying that sniping on the Bosnian Serb side, sniping from the Bosnian Serbs was stupid, and that it didn't get the Serbs any military advantage ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, yes. Well, I stand by that. This is what I remember Dr. Karadzic as saying. Of course you must --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But my question was whether you knew any sniping incident, what sniping Dr. Karadzic was referring to at that time? And you also continued to say that: "The same regards irresponsible shelling or instances when there was some shelling ..." So what kind of irresponsible shelling you discussed at the time? Could you expand on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot expand because I was talking about a conversation we had in which the subject was mentioned in general, not with particular reference to any particular events of sniping or shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By your answer about quote/unquote irresponsible -- I'm sorry, irresponsible shelling, we can take it that Dr. Karadzic had known some irresponsible shelling at least, at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he knew about it but he would -- I think he told me that, you know, there was some stupid officers who -- who were irresponsible, but I cannot remember any names or any particular event associated with that. But he was in general very critical of the army, I would say that. And you know, I got used to him saying, you know, that this general or this colonel is -- is not -- is not someone who is responsible or -- or general things like that, but I'm not referring to any particular events or any particular names. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I note the time. Shall we continue after a break? We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. If I could very briefly raise one housekeeping matter in connection with the pending resolution of the motions concerning either safe conduct or subpoena for Mr. Kijac. I simply wanted to note that irrespective one way or another of the outcome, that the parties have agreed that his projected date of appearance would be the first week of December and not the date previously indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zametica, I think that before the break the question had to do with what you noticed about our and especially my positions about the humanitarian needs of civilians in our territory and especially that of the other two warring parties. Were you in a position to notice what my position was to their humanitarian needs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I think you were very cooperative regarding the humanitarian needs, the humanitarian convoys, although you often complained about the attitude of the army, you even used rude language to describe their behaviour. So I think you were every now and again rather frustrated about the fact that the army was perhaps not as cooperative with regard to the passage of humanitarian convoys as you would have liked them to have been. Of course, in this context, I should also mention the fact that, to be fair to the Army of Republika Srpska, that they frequently detected illegal activities concerning those humanitarian convoys such as smuggling of arms. And perhaps they had every reason to oppose further passage of such convoys if they had reason to suspect or if they actually found that the humanitarian convoys were delivering goods other than goods meant to cover the humanitarian needs. I mean weapons. But, yeah, on the whole, I would say that you were cooperative with regard to that. I think the best example of that is the fact that -- I think it was in June 1992 when you agreed to the handing over of Sarajevo airport to the UN and on humanitarian grounds. Thereby, you gave up a military strategic advantage which the forces of Republika Srpska had in holding the airport, and which perhaps almost cost you the war. So that's what I would have to say in general on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica. Were there any examples of incidents after which certain corridors had to be closed down for commercial traffic? And what was our attitude to humanitarian convoys as opposed to commercial and other civilian traffic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Well, I remember one occasion in 1995, was it April or May of 1995, when you actually ordered a closure of the so-called blue routes, but that was in connection with the fact that, I think, two Serb girls were killed by Muslim snipers and there was much public outrage regarding that. I personally remember that because I saw it -- I saw the corpses of those two girls shown on TV and there was indeed much outrage about that. So you did react in that particular connection, I seem to remember, and ordered the closure of the routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D25093 in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this announcement of yours in the media, at the top of the page. Can you please tell us whether you remember this and whether this corresponds to what was going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Yes. I have no particular comment to make on that. That statement -- this statement corresponds to the situation at the time -- I don't -- I don't seem to see a date for that particular -- is this June 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] July, July.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: This is July 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you see this, apart from your words, when they convey what "Borba" reported about, and is that in accordance with information that you had that the civilian traffic was closed rather than humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before he answers the question, let's find out what this is about. Mr. Zametica, do you read the first line of this document, "Vecernje Novosti," 28th of July, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it on top of page, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a statement that I made regarding allegations by the Muslim side that -- that the Serb side was blockading humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is -- what was "Vecernje Novosti"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Vecernje Novosti" is a Belgrade mass circulation paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it this is an excerpt from that "Vecernje Novosti" written by Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you going to deal with the next page as well? Or shall we admit only this page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only this page, and only the first part, down to the next title. What Mr. Zametica said and what was reported by the "Borba" daily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3928, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, you recently mentioned accusations levelled against the Serbs. The false accusations for something that they were not in reality doing. Can you tell us what your experience was with that sort of game, how we were represented in the media, and did this representation correspond to what you could observe in our conduct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: That is the second very large question you have put to me regarding the media. I would say that the international media on the whole reported the Bosnian war in black and white terms, very -- in a very partisan way, supporting the Muslim side which was portrayed as the victim, and portraying the Serb side as the aggressor. That's what I would say in general. Few Western journalists came to Pale, few Western journalists came to Grbavica which was part of Sarajevo and which was Serb-held throughout the war -- throughout the war, or to Ilidza and other suburbs around Sarajevo that were held by the Bosnian Serb forces. Why this was so remains partly a mystery. Why did the Western media report in the way they did without bothering to -- to present a more researched, a more objective picture. There were exceptions, of course, but on the whole I think Western journalists were looking for ways in which to present this rather complex conflict, with complex origins, and with very complex goings-on. Remember there was not just one war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were two, three, at times four wars in Bosnia-Herzegovina, going on concurrently. The war between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Muslims, the war between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats, the war between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, the war between Muslims and Muslims in the Western region of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I think my impression was that Western journalists wanted to simplify matters. And in simplifying them and looking at the same time for a sort of good guys, bad guys, type of story, the Serbs were an easy target in the sense that for a lot of the time, the Bosnian Serb forces, military forces, held the military advantage or had the military advantage and the Bosnian Muslims were seen as the losing side. It did not help matters that the Bosnian Serbs were seen as an extended hand of the regime in Belgrade, in Serbia, an extended hand of Mr. Milosevic. You, yourself, are being portrayed to this very day, in many popular accounts, and even academic accounts of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina as the extended hand of Mr. Milosevic, which I find absurd. I cannot imagine a greater enemy, repeat enemy, of the Bosnian Serbs than Mr. Milosevic himself, together with his wife. So the Western journalists, in portraying the war in Bosnia as a kind of Serb aggression agreed between you and Mr. Milosevic, whose tool you were, according to their accounts, had a good story. This was swallowed, hook, line and sinker, by many people in the West. There were those, of course, who remained curious or critical, but on the whole, people relied in the West on what the mainstream media were telling them, and day after day, there were all these horror stories. I remember on quite a few occasions the Muslims were saying that the Bosnian Serb forces were shelling Sarajevo airport. That's why the humanitarian convoys couldn't get through, because the airport was under fire from the Serbs. Whereas, in fact, humanitarian convoys were also very good business for the Muslim side. We have the evidence from Phillip Corwin who served on the civilian side in Sarajevo with the UN, he worked for the UN, who in his diary wrote that he knew the Muslim side had often shelled, deliberately shelled, Sarajevo airport in order to stop the flights coming in, in order to make sure that the prices of goods that they were in the business of selling to the population of Sarajevo went up. So -- and the Serbs, Corwin continued, if I remember correctly, the Serbs were regularly being blamed by the Western media nor doing something that, in fact, the Muslims were doing in order to gain -- to gain financially from it. So this is just one illustration of the way in which the Western media were uncritically reporting events, in this case the shelling of Sarajevo airport, blaming it on the Serbs, whereas in fact, as we have learned from Phillip Corwin, but we knew that any way, but it's good to have someone neutral say that, it was the Muslims who were responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to help with the transcript, did you talk about Phillip Corwin?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Phillip Corwin, C-o-r-w-i-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you know that what Mr. Corwin wrote in his book was correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I read his book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did meet him, I think in 1995, several times in Pale. So I was in the meetings when he too was present, but of course he subsequently wrote his book, which is a combination of his diary and his subsequent reflections on the events. But most of it is actually what historians call primary evidence, i.e. diary material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zametica, you mentioned Karadzic and Milosevic as a context. In your view, was there some sort of agreement or joint enterprise or anything joint between these two political views and these two political tendencies, primarily between myself and President Milosevic, regardless of how much respect I have for him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I fail to see why you should feel you have to add regardless of how much you have respect for him. I think you should consider yourself lucky to be still alive, because he was going for you. I think at least since the Vance-Owen Plan, Mr. Milosevic was looking for ways to get rid of you, either politically or even physically. And together with his wife, who absolutely detested you, they were scheming to replace you with someone more pliable. Milosevic is often portrayed as a -- as the person who was scheming the creation of something called Greater Serbia. Nothing could be further from the truth. He was an unreformed communist, and all he was really interested in was to stay in power and consolidate his power. Serbs did not interest him. Serbs outside Serbia interested him even less. I would say that in Milosevic you had a very formidable enemy because he was in charge of a state which still had -- despite sanctions still had considerable military and economic potential and ways and means. As you know, following the failure of the Contact Group Plan, Milosevic it was who imposed sanctions on Republika Srpska. So a state that was under sanctions itself, Serbia, was imposing sanctions on Republika Srpska. We were cut off from the rest of the world. I think all that Milosevic was really concerned about was to, as hastily as possible, sell the Serbs outside Serbia down the river in order to lift the sanctions and be able to say to his people: "I have achieved this, despite all the difficulties. You can have confidence in me. We are going to build a great future together." He was certainly not interested in creating something called Greater Serbia. You were certainly not his tool. And I don't see why you should say you still have regard for that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we leave Milosevic aside, did you establish that there was some joint criminal enterprise on my side, that is to say, the side of myself and my associates?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I believe the answer to your question is implied in my answer to your previous question. So the idea --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: The idea of some kind of joint criminal enterprise between yourself and Mr. Milosevic is absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say whether you established or whether you observed that, on my part, on the part of the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs, the people I worked with, whether there was any enmity or any kind of inhumane position vis-à-vis Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Muslims and Croats as such, not some of them, like a political entity. Muslims and Croats as such.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Again, I believe that at least part of the answer to this particular question is implied in some of my previous answers, when I talked about your attitude towards me, someone who has a Muslim background. I don't think you were a man driven by ethnic hatred. I don't think you were a man driven by any dogma of that kind. That's simply not you. People who do not know you may -- people who have received a wisdom about you from newspapers or popular accounts about the war probably have a very different view about you, but I knew you very well, I worked very closely with you, and I don't think you had anything, even approaching in you that we could call ethnic hatred or feeling of ethnic superiority vis-à-vis the Muslims or the Croats, not at all. All you were concerned to achieve was a lasting and fair political and territorial settlement regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The very basis of the indictment against me, the very basis of the indictment, without which there would have been no indictment, contains a position to the effect that I wanted to get rid of Muslims and Croats from the territories that we thought we were entitled to, and entitlement to territory is not an incrimination. Did you notice that I personally or the responsible part of the leadership had the intention to get rid of Muslims and Croats from our areas, to expel them, even going all the way up to genocide? And would you turn a blind eye to that had you noticed something like that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No. I certainly think that you had no plans, schemes, in that direction at all. You were always going to be happy if Muslims and Croats stayed on the territory of Republika Srpska. You appointed, as far as I know, quite a few people in the judiciary system of Republika Srpska who were -- who had Muslim or Croat background. You appointed me as your principal aide in foreign affairs. I had a Muslim background. You had, I don't want to name him now in an open session, a person who was in a very sensitive position in Republika Srpska also had a Muslim background. Another person I remember who was also close to you had a Croat ethnic background. I mean, it doesn't make sense to call you someone who -- someone who -- who was -- who was driven by ethnic hatred in the light of what I know and what I experienced with you, what you were telling me. You, in fact, considered the Muslims to have been originally Serbs who then chose to become Muslims and you respected that. That was fine by you. What people in the West often failed to pay sufficient attention to is the fact that, in fact, we were fighting a defensive war. It was the Muslims, together with the Croats, but principally the Muslims who started the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And through a series of illegal actions in late 1991 and early 1992, actions that destroyed the political consensus in Bosnia and Herzegovina or I should say the remnants of political consensus in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The culmination of that was the illegal decision to hold the referendum on independence which took place in late -- end of February, beginning of March, 1992. On top of that, I should add that the political group leading the Muslims at the time was not Muslim nationalist. This was a group that I would call Muslim internationalist, led by Alija Izetbegovic and his clique. I say he was not a Muslim nationalist rather he was a Muslim internationalist, he was a pan-Islamist and his ideology was Islam. His politics were pan-Islamism. I'm just paraphrasing what he himself wrote in his book called "The Islamic Declaration," where he also stated that there can be no peace or co-existence between, on the one hand, Islam and on the other hand, non-Islamic -- non-Islamic organisations or non-Islamic society. And he also stated that the moment the Muslims feel themselves morally and numerically strong enough, they should overthrow the existing system and set up an Islamic one. At the meetings, I remember the meetings, pre-election meetings in October 1990, during the first free elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, his supporters at the SDA rallies, they had banners, for example, saying, "Long live Saddam Hussein." What I'm trying to say is that the politics of Mr. Izetbegovic who was the legally and legitimately Muslim -- elected Muslim representative, elected by a very large majority of the Muslim population, his politics and his plans were perceived by the Serb side as really threatening and really dangerous. Even so, you had agreed, as we have already said, to the Zulfikarpasic plan, to the Cutileiro Plan and so on and so forth. But I mean, I think people in the West often fail to pay enough attention to the threat that this man and his clique and his ideology and his proclaimed aims, the way we perceived them. And I think we fought a defensive war, I think we fought a just war, and I don't think we have anything to be ashamed of. Except one episode - I'm sure we'll come to that - and that's Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell us, as briefly as possible, whether, in addition to becoming familiar with the political papers of this leadership, did you have personal contacts with this leadership that followed Mr. Izetbegovic? I mean, in addition to Mr. Zulfikarpasic, who left him.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Well, I knew -- I knew Professor Muhamed Filipovic but I'm not sure whether he was -- he must have been together with Zulfikarpasic, with Izetbegovic in SDA. But apart from those two individuals, I didn't know any other prominent Muslim personalities. I knew Izetbegovic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move on to another topic now. Do you know, do you remember, what the mandate of UNPROFOR was and what our attitude was towards UNPROFOR and NATO, from the moment when they joined forces and when the bombing took place? Did you know what our position was, what UNPROFOR could do and what they could not and should not do?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: In answer to your question, I would like to cite or rather paraphrase, I can't remember exactly, but I would like to cite what Cedric Thornberry - Cedric, S-e-d-r-i-c [sic], Thornberry - said in his centenary lecture held at the London School of Economics in 1995. Cedric Thornberry was involved with the United Nations in Sarajevo in 1992, on the civilian side, a very respected personality. And several years later, as I said in 1995, he held this centenary lecture in which he stated, if my recollection is correct, that one of the main lessons to be drawn from the experience of international peacekeeping is that one must be clear that peacekeeping is peacekeeping, and enforcement is enforcement, and that there can be no hybrid or hybrid, I think he called it monstrous hybrid, in between. And I think this is what happened in May 1995, when the United Nations, through NATO, ceased to be a peacekeeper and became a war maker. The essence of international peacekeeping is to -- to stay neutral in a conflict. The idea is to try and keep peace, secure the passage of humanitarian convoys and so on. What happened in May 1995 was that this was thrown out of the window and the Serbs were bombarded. So the line was crossed, the line between peacekeeping and peacemaking had been crossed. Our attitude was very clear. We accepted the presence of UN forces on the ground, in fact we welcomed that, and when the -- when the threat became clear that UN might change its role and become a factor of enforcement, I remember very clearly that on several occasions we informed the representatives of the UN, both military and civilian, that in that event we should treat the UN as our enemy. I think the position was very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can you say in connection with our taking prisoner of UN personnel after the bombing started? What status did they have, in our opinion? What was communicated to them? And how were they treated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: The taking of UN personnel as prisoners or hostages had been announced in advance, but I personally disagreed with that. I thought that Republika Srpska, in 1995, was in a -- in a position of international isolation that was deep enough already. We didn't need further international isolation. And that any step that would lead to a breakdown of our relationships with the international community or, rather, with the UN in this particular case, could only worsen our position. So I was against it. At the same time, when the bombardment took place, feelings, popular feeling, feelings were running very high on the streets, and it is perhaps understandable that UN personnel on the ground were taken prisoner. But I felt this was -- this was an untenable position and, in fact, I remember writing a memorandum, I seldom used to write memoranda but I did write a memorandum very soon after the event, which was sometime after 25th of May, 1995, in which I argued for the immediate release of the UN prisoners. I think you agreed with me. I was knocking on an open door there. And indeed, all the prisoners were released very soon, and no harm was done to them. So -- well, I hope I have answered your question. I cannot remember its original phrasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we consider them to be hostages? Or were they there in some other capacity? And what was communicated to them? What was their position? Were they hostages or prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: They were treated as prisoners of war, but I think it was indicated to them that, you know, this is only a very temporary situation where they were going to be released very soon. I think the intention was never going to -- the intention was never to keep them as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in a position to establish the following? When we were asked to allow people to enter Gorazde or some other enclaves, were you in a position to find out what the specialty of these soldiers was? Were we deceived sometimes? Did some other people enter those areas, people who were not actually what they said they were? I have a statement of yours, a public statement that you made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a pretty leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right. I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you following this when we allowed them to enter, and was it always what it was declared to be? Were they just military observers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I remember a episode from 1994, around Gorazde, when some of those so-called military observers turned out to be FACs, forward air controllers. They are the people who guide an aircraft up in the air to its target on the ground. And I remember that particular -- as you say, I think I did give a -- I did make a statement about it but I cannot remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of May 1995, when these prisoners were taken, can you tell us whether it was envisaged or planned that these prisoners of war be threatened by punishment, by death or wounding? Do you know what was envisaged and do you know how they were treated actually?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: That was never said to them, as far as I know. I mean, no threats were made. I think -- I think they -- those of them who were subsequently interviewed by the Western media all said that they were well treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
