utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you mentioned Gorazde and you talked about exaggerations at one point and misrepresentations of consequences and victims.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we have a look at 1D25089 in e-court? Could it be zoomed in, please? And then we would like to have page 2. This is April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this statement of yours about this exaggeration, misrepresentation --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually could we zoom in seriously on the first part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned today as well that there were false reports, especially about Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could Dr. Karadzic please just keep an eye on how he phrases the question because at no point in today's transcript did this witness mention the word "exaggerations" and misrepresentation of consequences. That makes this a leading question. All Dr. Karadzic needs to do is show the witness the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise if it was leading. Could we please see the lower part first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you remember this statement of yours? And can you tell us what it refers to and how it fits into your overall experience?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Well, I vaguely remember this statement I made but, I mean, you don't have to take my word for it, you can read the memoirs of General Sir Michael Rose who says essentially the same thing. He was the UN military commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the upper part so that we can see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zametica, can you tell us whether this was an exception, and how often or how rarely did this kind of thing happen, namely that a false picture was portrayed to the public?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I think this matter must have been clarified in this Tribunal many times over already. I mean, you only have to remind yourself of the statements made by, I think he was then the Foreign Minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Haris Silajdzic, who at the beginning of the conflict -- I was still in London admittedly, but I very closely followed the events. At the beginning of the conflict he was claiming 200.000 Muslim dead. This was, you know, after two months of conflict. In the end, the total number of casualties on all sides was somewhere like 100.000. So these exaggerations on the part of the Muslims about the number of their dead or wounded, such exaggerations were commonplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit pages 1 and 2. Any objection before that, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, pages 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3929, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zametica, can you tell us about this exaggeration, misrepresentation, how it affected our confidence in what we heard, what was bandied about in public? Could we believe such allegations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. So you have to rephrase it or -- I'm not -- I'm not sure what you're trying to -- to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this affected our lack of confidence in sources and allegations of this kind? Could we continue to blindly trust everything that the media reported?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Well, of course not, but you were a politician, I was your presidential aide. I mean, we could not blindly trust everything that the media reported in any case. And particularly not in this case. I mean such exaggerations, if this is what you're trying to say, such exaggerations did nothing to boost our confidence in the -- in the objectivity of the media, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After I went into hiding, did we correspond occasionally? In other words, were you able to receive my messages or perhaps a letter or send me a letter? Especially regarding the adoption of the Law on Cooperation with the Tribunal, especially until that time? Were there any obstacles in that period?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we did have a correspondence whilst you were a fugitive. As far as I can remember, a lot of that correspondence pertained to private matters concerning my family or things like that. There was some political content to that, regarding the situation in Republika Srpska, the wider Balkan situation. But nothing very memorable about that correspondence, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up 65 ter 21578 in e-court? [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2 in Serbian, 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the second paragraph and in English it begins with the words: "You know very well what we were going through." Here, in this paragraph, the subject is the same as what you just said, the allegations in the media. Do you remember this passage in my letter where I considered, together with you, what had happened in Srebrenica? In 2001, did we know more than we had in 1995? And what were our speculations, what did we know exactly at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: You mean to ask what we knew about Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, what did we know about it in 2001, when I wrote this letter? Did you know more than I did? And does this reflect what I knew and what I thought at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: You always respected me. You never lied to me. I never felt that you -- you were being even economical with the truth regarding anything. You completely trusted me, and I completely trusted you. In this kind of private correspondence, you would be as sincere with me as you would be in our normal course of -- in the normal course of events. So if in 2001, if this is 2001, you wrote this about Srebrenica, I have no reason to believe that you were not sincere in saying that. So in 2001, we didn't know much more about Srebrenica than we knew in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just -- probably it's only me, but I didn't follow the relation between this paragraph and Srebrenica. If you could clarify, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, in this letter, I wrote to Mr. Zametica my thoughts, my speculations, my attempts to reconstruct the events on the basis of all that I had learned up to 2001. That is the importance of the letter and a good part of the letter refers to Srebrenica 1995. I am thinking aloud what exactly might have happened and who stands behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, more specifically the second sentence in that paragraph is what [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does it read?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It reads that: "When you add to all this the information on the arrest of the Spider Group and the role of the French intelligence service in the events in Srebrenica, then it becomes crystal clear that we had nothing to do with it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I tender this whole letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This includes two letters from you? Before that, yes, do you have any observation or do you object, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Although I don't agree with Dr. Karadzic's characterisation of the contents of the letter, I have no objection to the whole 17 pages, two letters, being tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So are you tendering it in its entirety, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It could be. I have here from one to five but it could be all 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the Prosecution position, we will admit it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3930, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we come to this point. Looking at the agendas kept by my secretaries, I see that we had encounters between 10 and 14 July, on several occasions, and these meetings were also attended by Dr. Trifkovic, et cetera. Do you remember coming to my office on certain dates in July 1995, that you met me at my office?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: For God's sake we had daily contact in those -- I mean, frequent daily contact during those days. I was -- I left Pale, I think, on the 19th of July because I had to be present at my own wedding. But until that date, we were in frequent daily contact. Yes, of course I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Chamber what did we know at that point in time about events around Srebrenica, especially after the takeover of Srebrenica? What information did we have at our disposal?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: We knew that a military operation had been successfully completed, the military operation of neutralising Srebrenica as a military stronghold from which the Muslims were frequently staging attacks. Not only on our forces but also on our civilians. That much we knew. If you are asking me did we know something about a massacre that took place in Srebrenica during roughly that period, then my answer is we knew nothing about that. By "we," I mean the civilian side. I mean you, I mean myself, I mean our close colleagues in the Presidency. We knew nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we pause here? Just going back to the previous document, which we admitted as D3930, Ms. Edgerton, is it your intention to use the other part of the letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I haven't decided yet, Your Honour, to be perfectly honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, we are going to admit only the page which was shown to the witness. Yes. And, Mr. Robinson, if you could remind me, remind us whether we heard ever the evidence about or in relation to Pauk or Spider Group?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know if that term has been used for sure. It's possible that it has been but I don't recall exactly. I think that that was a designation of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, but I don't know whether or not that has ever been actually testified to by a witness or is contained in a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, I don't think that's correct. But I'm not able to give Your Honours any further information about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I have to ask Mr. Zametica whether he remembers anything about -- anything related to the arrest of Pauk or Spider Group. Can you assist us, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can remember, Your Honour, I can remember reading about it in the press, in the media. It was a big story. I didn't follow it very closely so I'm afraid I cannot assist you in any significant way. But it -- at the time I remember it was quite a big story. So maybe Mr. Karadzic can elaborate on that, but I don't have the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I will leave it at that. Shall we continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellency, if it's of any assistance, I can say that we have evidence here that the 10th Sabotage Detachment members were taken by the French to Africa to fight, and later they were involved in attempts to kill Milosevic. But the connection is that these people were members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. And then, after our war, they were taken to Africa to fight, and then they were -- they reappeared as the Pauk, Spider Group, and arrested by the Serbian intelligence service, and caught in the attempt to kill Milosevic. Some gold was involved and some foreign party, foreign intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue? We'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zametica, as opposed to what we knew, how was all this portrayed in the media? Did we have reason to trust media reports? Did we run our own checks? What were we able to establish during those days regarding the rumours surrounding Srebrenica? Were they true or not? I mean, before you left to attend your wedding, while you were there, did we check allegations published in the media and what did we conclude? First of all, was there any talk at that time about execution of prisoners or did it concern civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the last bit of your question. There was certainly no talk about executions of prisoners. I mean -- or anybody else for that matter, so, you know, I -- I can certainly say that much. But I'm not sure what -- what exactly you were asking there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you make a public statement or a press release regarding these allegations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I -- I -- I made a statement, I believe on the 17th of July, 1995, with regard to the media allegations that there had been mistreatment of prisoners. So, yes, I -- I denied that, and I denied that on the basis of the knowledge accessible to me, and to you by the way, at the time, and also on the basis of a declaration signed by the representative of Muslim civil authorities in Srebrenica - I cannot remember his exact name, someone called Nesim Mandzic or something like that - who, on that same day, 17 July, if I remember correctly, signed a declaration to the effect that the Muslim civilians from the area of Srebrenica had been well treated and had been evacuated, I believe he said, under the supervision of United Nations forces. There was no maltreatment of them and everything had been done in accordance with an agreement or -- yeah, it was an agreement of, I think, the 12th of July, which the Srebrenica authorities had signed with the representatives of the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we pull up 65 ter 25314 in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report by AFP on your communique. Please look at it. It says that allegations of torture, murder, rape, and deportation of Muslim civilians are made repeatedly without any independent verification, and then you mentioned this document signed on the 17th by the Muslims and the UNPROFOR. Is this what you just talked about? And how does this refutation upon verification fit in with the whole story of passing off misinformation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Well, yes. That is the statement I made. I remember it. I can only repeat that I made that statement on the basis of information available to us at the time. I have nothing further to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please answer the second part of my question. How does this reverified and reconfirmed exaggeration about the deportation and -- of civilians fit in with the context of what you just said? To what extent were the media to be believed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Yes. The -- it certainly was part of my experience that the Muslim side, as we have discussed already, would tend to exaggerate matters regarding their casualties. I remember already, at the beginning of the military operation Srebrenica, Muslim media, Haris Silajdzic, I seem to remember him particularly, listening to the Muslim radio, was shouting murder, was shouting rape. You know, the operation was still going on. He could not have known anything about what was happening. And in typical fashion, he had already decided that there had been horrible things going on at the time. So, yes, to answer your question, it was part of my experience that they would, as a matter of policy, exaggerate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go back to Mr. Karadzic's question. He said, I quote, "reverified and reconfirmed exaggeration about the deportation." Do you agree that you, the Bosnian Serbs, at the time, reverified or reconfirmed the Muslim argument or the statement at the time? And if yes, then how?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic was asking me whether it was part of my daily experience that, to hear, to listen to the Muslim side exaggerating about their casualties. I think he meant that. I think the way in which this particular question put by Dr. Karadzic was phrased is not -- not particularly clear, to me at least. So I would need -- I would need -- I would have to ask Dr. Karadzic to rephrase this question. I mean, there was no question that we thought anything horrible was going on. We thought everything was being done in accordance with all the conventions. I remember the late Professor Koljevic telling me at some stage during Operation Srebrenica, that General Mladic had told him he had let in the International Red Cross into the Srebrenica area. And I remember this particular episode precisely because at the time, Professor Koljevic was very angry with General Mladic because he thought General Mladic was taking away his job from him. Professor Koljevic was in charge of the International Red Cross and such organisations. So that's why I remember that particular episode. But it just illustrates that if I knew and if Dr. Karadzic knew that General Mladic had let in the International Red Cross into the Srebrenica area, plus this statement signed by what's his name, the Muslim civilian representative in Srebrenica, all of that formed a picture in our minds that everything was, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's leave it there. But my question was whether there is any process of reconfirmation or reverification of what happened in Srebrenica. But let's leave it to Mr. Karadzic. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I please have some water? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Dr. Zametica, who sent us this document and at whose request? How did we receive it? How did we receive this document confirming that all of this was regular?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, I cannot say that I do remember the exact circumstances about the receipt of this document. You have to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name Deronjic and the man's position? Was it at my request that this response came or would it have been sent by the Muslim authorities even if I had not requested it? Perhaps you don't know the details, but do you remember that there was the Bosnian Serb signature and the Muslim signature and the UNPROFOR's as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. The document dated 17 -- the Srebrenica document dated the 17th of July was signed by all three sides, by the Muslim side, by the Serb side, and by the UN. And the name Deronjic, I don't think I ever met the man, but I remember him, I remember that name, because I think he was the man you appointed at some stage during the Srebrenica military operation, possibly towards the end, as -- as the Serb civilian representative there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to have this document admitted. My point, Your Excellencies, was that this was a response to our verifications. Dr. Zametica did not have to know that we had asked Deronjic about the media reports and whether they were true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zametica, thank you very much that you came to testify although you are a very busy man and thank you for your long years of cooperation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 21578 will be Exhibit D3931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break for 45 minutes, after which we will hear the cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. But before we continue, please bear in mind, Mr. Zametica, although Ms. Edgerton and you will speak the same language, please put a pause for the benefit of Mr. Karadzic, who will hear in Serbo-Croat. Yes, there is one matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just for the record, the correct 65 ter number for Exhibit D3931 is 25314. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, I would like to start your cross-examination today by showing you 65 ter number 25545, page 1. And, Mr. Zametica, this is a copy of the e-mail that you wrote to Mr. Robinson on 28 June of this year, and that e-mail was appendixed to the public motion Dr. Karadzic filed on July 2nd for a subpoena for you to testify in his defence. And I just want to draw your attention to paragraph 2 of this e-mail. And in paragraph 2, you write that earlier that day, you were listing through a pile of documents which an intern had brought you after you signed your statement. And you say one of those documents flatly contradicts a central claim you make in your statement, one that you sincerely believed to be true when you wrote the statement, and the Prosecution would have no problem ripping apart this claim. So I'd like you, Mr. Zametica, to tell me the central claim you made in your signed statement that you now say was flatly contradicted by the document. And if you want, actually, we can have a look -- rather than have you look at notes, we can have a look at your signed statement in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 1D09616. And you can collapse the e-mail so that Mr. Zametica can see his statement at greater magnification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can go through this and you can identify for us the central claim that was contradicted by the document. Can we do that? Can you identify for us what it is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Yes, I can. If we go down to relations with the UN, I think that's how I entitled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have a hard copy? It's a 17-page document, I take it. Shall we print it? Oh, you have it, yes. Unless the Defence has problem with it, we'll hand it over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you go to page 13 of my statement, paragraph 27, near the bottom, so it's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm afraid, we have different version. But paragraph 27 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paragraph 27, fifth line from the bottom, sentence reads: "But there had been no policy decision to that effect." This is what I wrote. "But there had been no policy decision to that effect." Meaning -- I meant to say, and I think it's clear from the context if you read the whole paragraph, that there had been no decision by the leadership of Republika Srpska to take UN personnel prisoners. All right? So on returning from -- as you know, I was here already in June, but some other witness's testimony took much longer than expected and I never testified in June. In the meantime, I was handed a small pile of documents which were made available to the Defence by the Prosecution, and at home, having returned from The Hague, I had a closer look at those documents. One of those documents, which I don't have, unfortunately, with me today, but you have it because you made it available to the Defence, relates to an intercepted telephone conversation dated, I believe, the 30th -- the night of 30th to 31st May 1995. It is clear from that conversation, which was -- which involved several people, the call was made by Todor -- Mr. Todor Dutina, who was the Republika Srpska representative in Moscow. The call had been made either to Mr. Krajisnik or to Dr. Karadzic, I'm not sure which, and it's not, I think, clear from that document. But in that document, Mr. Krajisnik at one point says, in reply to Mr. Dutina's assertion that the international community is monitoring everything that the leadership of Republika Srpska is doing, and knows every single move that the Republika Srpska leadership is making or is about to make, in response to that assertion by Mr. Dutina, Mr. Krajisnik says: "How come, then, they didn't know we were going to do this?" From the context, it is clear, how come they didn't know we are going to do this, how come, in other words, they didn't know that we were going to take UN personnel prisoners? Any reasonably capable Prosecution could conclude that there was, in fact, a policy decision to the effect that UN personnel would be taken prisoner, in case of aerial attacks. I didn't know about that telephone conversation, but in the intercepted document, Dr. Karadzic mentions me twice because he too was -- I think they put on the speakerphone so they could all talk, mentions me two times, saying that "Zametica is speaking on my behalf or in my name," words to that effect. Now, what does all this mean? Any Prosecution could establish that, in fact, either Zametica is lying or he's a fool being fooled by the Republika Srpska leadership, or in any case, I turn out very badly from this, and that is why I objected. It's the business and duty of the Defence team to notify me of such evidence of which I was not aware when I wrote this statement. I wrote it in all sincerity, and I believed that there had been no decision, policy decision, to take UN personnel prisoner. So I objected and protested because I thought, for God's sake, this sort of thing is being discussed in court all the time, presumably, and the Defence should have let me know, having read my statement, they didn't write it on my behalf, I wrote it. Had they read it carefully they would have come across this sentence, "but there had been no policy decision to that effect," and said to me, look, this is wrong, there had been a policy decision to that effect. So I thought, as I wrote subsequently in this paragraph, my understanding is that a group of Russian volunteers, fighting on our side and stationed in Pale, had taken the initiative to start taking -- that is the reason why I wrote that -- what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this line, which doesn't say, "I believe there had been no policy decision to that effect" but says, "There had been no policy decision to that effect," is not true?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: What is truth? I don't think Dr. Karadzic deliberately misled me. I simply wasn't there. This was at night time. I was up in my hotel on -- ten kilometres away on Mount Jahorina. There clearly, according to Mr. Krajisnik, had been some kind of decision to that effect. I hadn't been notified of that, but this was a fast-moving situation. I -- I would normally have been notified of such things, but I was sincerely unaware of that particular decision, in whatever form it was taken. Whether it was spontaneously immediately after the first bombs fell or whether it was subsequently, I certainly was not privy to that decision and I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But the very next sentence -- now you've just said you weren't there, you didn't know about it, but your very next sentence reads: "Karadzic had not issued any order about taking UN personnel prisoners." Is that also untrue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: As far as I knew it, yes -- as far as I knew it, it was -- it was true. I thought that Karadzic had not issued such orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, again, Mr. Zametica, you wrote this in absolutes. You said: "Karadzic had not issued any order ..."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now you're qualifying what you wrote in your signed statement in June.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, it's not right. I'm not qualifying anything. I just gave you a very long explanation or I gave this Tribunal a very long explanation of the context in which I wrote what I wrote in my statement. And I repeat, at the time, I thought that there had been no policy decision to that effect. Having said that, and I think I mentioned this during the time when Dr. Karadzic earlier today questioned me, there had been warnings, so it did -- you know, this does not come as a surprise to me, that intercepted document, not as a huge surprise, because there had been warnings to the UN, if you bomb, there will be consequences, we will treat you as an enemy. Of course, taking UN personnel prisoner would have been a consequence of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, what about this next sentence, which says your understanding is that a group of Russian volunteers fighting on your side had taken the initiative to start taking hostages. So is your understanding that four military corps, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps, the East Bosnia Corps, the Drina Corps - oh, actually five - and the 2nd Krajina Corps were all separately prompted to take UN personnel hostages and place them at military targets and VRS military facilities right across the areas of responsibilities of all five of them because of something a group of Russian volunteers did?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: That was my understanding. I was given this information about a group of Russian volunteers by the then Minister of Information, Mr. Miroslav Toholj. And my understanding was that when this initial action of Russians taking UN personnel prisoner started in Pale, there was an avalanche effect. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look at D2149 next, please. This is a Defence Exhibit, not yet, a Defence Exhibit D2149 tendered by Dr. Karadzic and it was offered by General Milovanovic relating to his meetings with Dr. Karadzic, between May 1992 and December 1995. And I'd like us to go over to page 56 in the English and page 38 in the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, just a second. Yes, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would kindly request if the English version can be enlarged because I can hardly read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you mind, then, if we collapse the Cyrillic version so you can just read at least one of them clearly --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Well, for the time being I don't mind, but I certainly cannot read the small letters there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if at any time you want to see the Cyrillic of a --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- document or the other version, just say. So here, on the entry in this diary for May 25th, 1995, on the very last line, General Milovanovic says: "While informing Karadzic about the start of bombardment, he," and if we go over to the next page, "he ordered me to activate last year's decision of the Supreme Command on the VRS arresting everything foreign in RS territory." So not only was there a policy decision taken by the RS leadership, your understanding of Dr. Karadzic's role in the operation is actually incorrect. Dr. Karadzic ordered it, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: It is possible, yes. I cannot confirm that or deny that. I think it is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, how about if we go over to - your indulgence for a moment - P2137, which is a VRS Main Staff order to the commands of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the air force, the anti-aircraft defence, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the East Bosnia Corps, all the corps, signed by General Milovanovic. Now, have a look at this document, Mr. Zametica. It says in paragraphs 1 and 2, that the corps commands and the air force and anti-aircraft defence shall, in agreement with the commanders of the logistics bases, place the captured UNPROFOR staff as well as the staff of other international humanitarian organisations in their AORs in the areas of command posts, firing positions, and other potential targets that may come under air strike. And then, if you go over in the English translation to page 2, paragraph 8, and also find the second-to-last paragraph in the original B/C/S, you see, Mr. Zametica, that this order of the VRS Main Staff about the deployment of UNPROFOR has been approved by the president of the Republika Srpska. Mr. Zametica, not only is it possible, that's what the evidence shows. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: That is what General Milovanovic says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's what this order shows. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No. I'm not trying to say this is impossible. All I'm saying, this is what General Milovanovic was saying. There is no direct connection between his document and Dr. Karadzic saying these people should be tied up to, I don't know, posts and the like. It is possible. I -- I have no knowledge of that and I cannot comment on it. But all I'm saying is that you do not actually prove a direct connection here. This is what Milovanovic says.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So evidence that the specific order deploying UNPROFOR personnel to military locations that could be the subject of NATO air strikes has been approved by the president of the Republika Srpska doesn't in your mind represent a direct connection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, it does not because -- because the army would do very often things on its own regardless of Dr. Karadzic's wishes or orders or instructions. As I said earlier, the army was very much on its own, pursuing its own policy. I'm not saying this is impossible. All I'm saying, it proves nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could have a look at another document, please. It's D1055.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you call that up, if we could go over to page 5, which is a statement given by you on 26 May 1995, at midnight, actually, 26 May 1995, in response to the air strikes. And you said there,

utterances.speaker: MR. ZAMETICA
utterances.text: "I believe that we have demonstrated" -- you can read it halfway down the page. "We have demonstrated our determination and firmness through today's response," and you describe it as a restrained response, and that the international community will understand that. You also say: "However, if that's not understood and the attacks continue, we shall go further. If the international community continues with the use of force, we shall respond in the same manner. We are defending ourselves in our traditional territories and we will respond adequately to the use of force." And just to put things in context, the first air strike took place at 4.20 on 25 May 1995. All the safe areas were shelled except for Zepa, and the source for that is P6275 --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, no, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- and -- and here you are, using language that speaks expressly of unity of purpose and unity of action, Mr. Zametica. How is the army doing something on their own?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: If you go further up in this document, which is my statement dated 26th of May, you will see that I'm sending here a signal to the international community which is as follows. I'm reading now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can see the document, Mr. Zametica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say that: "The international community has so far demonstrated a total lack of understanding. We are defending ourselves in our traditional territories," and I continue further down. "We are prepared to negotiate today or tomorrow, but only on the basis which would assure equal treatment to us as to the other parties to this conflict." So my message there -- of course, I said all these things. I'm not denying it for a second. And it was a strong statement, and you must understand the context in which it was made. Feelings were running very high. But the most important part of this document is the one where I'm sending a signal to the international community, hey, we are prepared to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was about the language you used. You said, referring to the -- what you described as a restrained response, you said, "We, we, we," over and over. Are you saying that this was the army doing something on their own?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I'm not saying that. All I'm saying is that you -- you cannot demonstrate what you call unity of purpose here. There was no unity of purpose. There may have been a coincidence of purpose but never something as grand as what you have termed the unity of purpose. Didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying now that it's a coincidence that all the safe areas were shelled within hours of the first air strike? It's only a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Your question doesn't follow from my answer. I don't see the logical connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe you could answer my question. Are you saying it's a coincidence that all NATO safe areas were -- pardon me, all safe areas were shelled within hours of the first NATO air strikes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: The question of coincidence does not arise here at all. I fail to follow your logic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was the army doing something off their own bat?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Very often that was the case. I don't know what the army was doing in this particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then why do you use the words "we" all the way through your response that's carried across the world?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Because it is logical that I say "we." What other term in the English language would you have recommended me to use?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll move on. The next day, after all the safe areas were shelled, and you issue this threat that "we" will go further, you up the ante and that -- on the 26th of May, within one hour from the second air strike, you were shelling Sarajevo with 250-kilo air bombs, you blocked land access to Sarajevo, you cut the water and electricity supplies off, and you reacted by taking human shields. The order that Dr. Karadzic gave to General Milovanovic was implemented all across the country. That's what happened, isn't it, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: That is what you said happened. I'm not so sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you were there. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: How many human shields, if I may ask, were there out of, I don't know, 300 prisoners? Because I mean -- sorry, I just need to continue. What you said sounded as if, if someone didn't know about it, as if all prisoners were human shields. In fact, a very small proportion of prisoners were human shields. Not that I approved of it. I made my opposition to the whole idea very clear earlier on. But I just wonder why you are using language which suggests that all prisoners, all UN prisoners, were human shields, which was demonstrably not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, I gave you the context and the sequence of events and you said that you weren't so sure this is what happened. So if I'm wrong, I'd like you to tell me what happened. You were there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: The fact that I was there doesn't mean that I knew everything that was happening. So whatever happened there, and my knowledge about those events, I have related in my statement and I have nothing further to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zametica, let's look at something else you said on 26 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 25339.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's your press statement carried by Reuters.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And perhaps we could enlarge it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd like you to go down to the second-to-last sentence. It says: "Zametica said that the Serbs have positioned UN troops and unarmed military observers around potential targets that NATO might hit." Well, Mr. Zametica, based on what you say at the time, not only were you there, you knew these military observers had been deprived of their weapons, deprived of their protective gear, dispersed throughout Serb-held territory to compel NATO forces to stop the air strikes. And In fact, you say -- if you go up and look at the second paragraph on that page, you say: "If it wishes to proceed, the international community as a whole will have to pay a very, very heavy price." And further, you say: "It will not stop at that. The Serbs are determined to make a point to the entire world." And very -- at the very bottom of the page, you say: "If the NATO alliance wishes to continue with air strikes, then it will have to kill the UN troops here on the ground." You were there, you knew exactly what was going on, Mr. Zametica. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I think I made my views on the subject very clear earlier on. I personally opposed the whole policy of taking UN personnel prisoner. The Reuters report which you have presented me with sounds very much like -- like a made-up statement, in part at any rate. It sound to me like some kind of briefing I may have given to some journalists, there were plenty of journalists there at the time, but off the record. I never would use terms like: "It will have to kill the UN troops here on the ground." I was very aware -- but that in particular sounds to me like a made-up story. I was very much aware of the importance of communicating with the Western media, with the Western world. I was very careful in my choice of words and I would never have used words to that effect or the words that are stated here. So, yes, I was there, I'm not denying that I was there, but I didn't know everything that was taking place. Fast-developing situation, plenty of emotion. War, you see, is not a set of rational moves and countermoves. Emotion comes into it. Fear comes into it. And so on. So this was one of those situations. But I, despite the statement which we saw earlier on, which I'm not denying I'm the author of, this sounds to me like an off-the-record briefing with an additional content thrown in, of which I'm not the author. I would never have used things -- terms like: "It will have to kill the UN troops." That would have been a completely wrong message to send to the international community. I drew your attention just earlier on now to the most important part of my statement of, I think, 26th of May, where I said that Republika Srpska is prepared to negotiate. Do you think that I was unaware of the very situation -- very serious situation in which we were finding ourselves? I mean, our only hope was through negotiations. Our only hope was, you know, given the combined forces arranged against us, which were enormous, from the international community to the Western media, to Mr. Milosevic and his wife in Belgrade, to the insubordinate army, to -- our only hope was to have a peace settlement as fast as possible. So -- so this statement which you have presented -- this press -- Reuters press report completely goes against my thinking at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've just once again described the army as insubordinate, but, Mr. Zametica, we've looked at a series of documents now, including military documents, that show exactly the contrary, that show the army is implementing a directive, an order, in fact, from Dr. Karadzic. On what basis, in respect of this operation, are you claiming the army is insubordinate now?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Can you show me that order by Dr. Karadzic? Not Milovanovic's document, Dr. Karadzic's document. Is there one?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have seen the evidence from General Milovanovic's diary. If you'd like, I can call it back up for you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No. I have seen it. I asked you to give to me, to demonstrate to this Tribunal Dr. Karadzic's order. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, I've just told you, you've already seen the evidence. Now you can answer my question. On what basis, in respect of this operation, are you now claiming the army is insubordinate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: The army was insubordinate all the time. It was preparing a military putsch in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I asked you --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I can go -- I can go into detail. I mean, an army that is preparing a putsch --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, stop. I'm not asking you about August. I specifically asked you about this operation.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Well, what makes you think that during this operation, the army was acting as, all of a sudden, an instrument of the political leadership of Republika Srpska and had become less independent than it normally was?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, you're not answering my question, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me put this. What is your evidence,

utterances.speaker: MR. ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Number 1, Dr. Karadzic never ordered the taking prisoners of UN soldiers or, number 2, you did not know whether he issued such orders or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for a moment, and I'll go on to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could admit this exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course. That would make understanding Mr. Zametica's answers much easier. If that could be a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6474, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've mentioned a couple of times today, both to Dr. Karadzic and to your answers to me, about the memorandum you wrote advocating the release of the hostages and that was because you thought there was a risk of additional international isolation. Fair?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Fair enough, but that's not the whole story. I felt that taking prisoner -- taking UN personnel prisoner was also morally unsustainable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, it looks like -- your indulgence for a moment. Now, Dr. Koljevic, who you referred to in your signed statement a couple of times, wrote about your memo in his diary actually, and I assume you've read his diary. Have you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I have read parts of his diary. It is a diary which has been published, in two very large tomes. I would not like to claim that I have read it from page 1 to the last page. I have read bits of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Then you knew that Dr. Koljevic had written about your memo in his diary. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I cannot remember now but it's very possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter number 25569.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which is an excerpt from his diary, or the excerpt from his diary which talks about your memo. And in the B/C/S original it's at pages 152 and 153. And you can just tell us, Mr. Zametica, which you'd like to have on the screen in front of you, the English or the B/C/S. I'd like you to direct your attention to the paragraph that reads: "On that same day, 29 May," because that's the part that relates to your memorandum. And if you can skim through that, I'm going to take you over to the next page and then I'm going to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we collapse the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is that all right with you, Mr. Zametica? Shall we collapse the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us when we can go to the next page, Mr. Zametica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And there is going to be part of a third page after that. So let us know when you've come to the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you talked about your memo --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't finished reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let me ask the question and you can continue reading after I ask the question. When you talked about your memo, Mr. Zametica, you didn't mention this next bit that Dr. Koljevic has written about in his book, and it was about a proposal, your proposal, as regards the eastern enclaves. Now have a read.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, what you didn't mention is that you also made a proposal for an immediate fierce offensive attack against the eastern enclaves at the same time as UNPROFOR members were released selectively, and you pointed out that that would be the only move that would bring us back to the negotiating table to ensure a complete victory in Eastern Bosnia. Now, you relied on Dr. Koljevic's diary on more than one occasion in your signed statement. Can we also rely on Dr. Koljevic's diary in his rendering of your proposal to the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: To a large extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Great. Then I want to ask you a little bit about this fierce offensive against the eastern enclaves that you recommended at the end of May 1995. And what I'd like to know, Mr. Zametica, and it actually relates to something you said earlier today. You told Dr. Karadzic in your examination-in-chief that you didn't read the intelligence reports because he had advisors who did that, and you identified them. Now, do you agree, then, with the security advisor that did read those reports, that the killings in Srebrenica are a myth? In fact, he used the words, "a big farce." Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Before I say what my position is, I would like to have additional -- I would like to have clarification on who you're referring to and what is the -- what is the citation -- who are you attributing this citation to about the myth?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm attributing it to Ambassador Milinic who was one of the two advisors to Dr. Karadzic and he said this when he came to testify in Dr. Karadzic's Defence at this Tribunal at transcript pages 39769 to 70, and 39793.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I'm not responsible for what Gordan Milinic was saying, so I'm not clear what you're trying to ask me. I mean, are you asking me to comment on what Mr. Milinic said in his testimony? Is that what you're trying to ask me?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm asking you -- you said you didn't read any intelligence reports and Dr. Karadzic had advisors who did. Well, one of the people who read those said the killings at Srebrenica are a myth, a farce. Is that your position as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, it is not my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, then, Mr. Zametica, when you talk about the crimes at Srebrenica, as you did with Dr. Karadzic, you're talking about the mass executions of thousands of Bosnian men and boys by the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question? I'm not following you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So since that's not your position, I want to ask you if we can agree on this. When you talk, as you did in your examination-in-chief and in your written statement, actually, your signed statement, about the crimes at Srebrenica, you're talking about the mass execution of thousands of Bosnian men and boys by the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm just taking a little bit more time to come to the -- to the Srebrenica section, to see what exactly I wrote. I actually wrote - this is page 16, paragraph 35 - to this day, I do not know who perpetrated or ordered the crimes of -- the crimes in Srebrenica, but it is certain that whoever it was did a great disservice to Republika Srpska. That's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. When you talk about the crimes at Srebrenica, it's correct that you're referring to the mass executions of thousands of Bosnian Muslim men and boys by forces of the Republika Srpska. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No. First of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Tell us what you're referring to, then.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I'm referring to a massacre that took place in Srebrenica during that period. That's what I'm referring to. More than that, I cannot refer to because I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, there has been -- and you would know this because you seem to have been following the trials at this Tribunal rather closely. There has been several trials now into the allegations related to Srebrenica and there has been several findings about these executions and those findings are -- are to this effect: Those findings refer to 7.000 -- pardon me, those findings refer to almost 7.000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys executed by the armed forces of the Republika Srpska, the VRS and the MUP. Is it your evidence that you're not prepared to accept that as true?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not saying that. Incidentally, I wonder on what basis you say that I have been closely following the trial -- the trial here. I don't think this follows from anything I said. But as regards the massacre that took place in Srebrenica during that period that we are talking about, I can only repeat what I said in my statement in paragraph 35, and I shall read it to you again because you do not seem to have understood my -- so if you require additional explanations, I shall -- I shall be happy to try and provide them. But I repeat this first sentence in paragraph 35, which is as follows: To this day I do not know -- so to this day, and this was dated, I suppose in June -- to this day I do not know who, repeat who, perpetrated or ordered the crimes in Srebrenica, but it is certain that whoever it was did a great disservice to Republika Srpska. I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So can we take from what you're saying that you're not prepared to accept that almost 7.000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys were executed by the armed forces of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Once again, I repeat because you do not -- I don't know in which language I should be talking to you, but it seems to me that either you have chosen to misunderstand my English or ignore it, or perhaps if I offer additional explanations -- but I think the -- the phrasing of this sentence, first sentence in paragraph 35, is as clear as it can be in the English language. So all I can say is that I was not in Srebrenica at the time. My knowledge at the time was that nothing in terms of crimes had been done in Srebrenica. That was also what I believe to this day was Dr. Karadzic's information. So I was not there, I do not know who, repeat who, perpetrated or ordered the crimes in Srebrenica. I'm sure this Tribunal has been looking into the matter very carefully and it will, I'm sure, establish the facts of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because you're not answering my question, I'll ask you one more thing in a slightly different way and then we'll move on. You refer repeatedly now, because you keep repeating something you wrote in your statement, to a massacre at Srebrenica. How many victims, to your knowledge, and do you believe, resulted from those executions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of the subject. Let me just add, because I see what you're driving at, let me repeat, I was not there on the spot. I have no idea what happened there except that it is by now clear something awful did happen. I don't know who perpetrated the crime. I don't know how many people were executed. So I'm not trying to run away from this subject. I'm just trying to be as clear as I can be in the English language, to tell you that I have no specific knowledge of the matter. I don't know how many people were executed. Even if only one was executed, that would have been wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also said today that as regards the massacre at Srebrenica, and you said this at temporary transcript page 50, that we didn't know any more in 2001, at the time you and Dr. Karadzic were having some private correspondence while he was a fugitive from justice, you didn't know any more in 2001 than was known in 1995. Mr. Zametica, Radislav Krstic, the deputy commander of the Drina Corps, was convicted here, at the ICTY, after a trial in the first instance in August 2001 of aiding and abetting in the genocide, murder, extermination, and persecutions in respect of the killing of thousands of Bosnian Muslim men and boys. So how can you say we didn't know any more in 2001 than we did in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: If the Tribunal convicted General Krstic, did you say? It must have investigated the matter very carefully, and I cannot comment on that. I think what you're referring to -- this is the private letter that Dr. Karadzic wrote to me in 2001. You will be aware that the subject of Srebrenica is still a subject of considerable controversy, and presumably what Dr. Karadzic meant to say in that letter is that basically we don't know now, in 2001, much more than we knew in 1995. Presumably that's what he meant but I cannot -- I cannot comment more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for a moment. Now, you said in response to a question by Dr. Karadzic earlier today as to what information we, referring to, I presume, you, he and other people, had at your disposal, your response was: "We knew that a military operation had been successfully completed, the military operation of neutralising Srebrenica as a military stronghold." Mr. Zametica, this was an operation ordered by Dr. Karadzic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: I believe it was, yes. However, I have something to add to that. I think when we are talking about Srebrenica, it is important to realise that there are two separate aspects to Srebrenica which most people seem to be unable to distinguish between. The first aspect of Srebrenica is military operation Srebrenica. The neutralising of a military stronghold, Srebrenica, bristling with armed people who are jumping out of it all the time, something that was commented upon by UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, in contravention to the demilitarisation agreement on Srebrenica. So the taking out of this military threat, Srebrenica, is aspect number 1 of the subject of Srebrenica. Aspect number 2 of Srebrenica is the massacre in or at Srebrenica. They are two very separate matters. Whoever did the crime, it was done on the ground, repeat, on the ground, and not as a result of some joint criminal enterprise. If it was, as you said, the Army of Republika Srpska that did it, then it was an army out of Dr. Karadzic's control. Repeat, out of Dr. Karadzic's control. I'm sure that Dr. Karadzic would have sanctioned aspect 1 of Srebrenica, which is the military operation. I'm equally convinced, however, that he would never have sanctioned any crimes that subsequently took place in or around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look at another document. Now, you said, when I asked you, that you believe that the military operation of neutralising Srebrenica was ordered by Dr. Karadzic. Now, I'd like you to have a look at P4484. And it's going to take us some steps to go through this. This is an excerpt from a dictaphone tape containing a number of recorded conversations and I want you to look at a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and the Drina Corps commander, General Zivanovic about the attack on Srebrenica. And it's dated on or around July 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 8 July, on or around 8 July 1995. Let's have a look at the conversation. A third of the way down the page, Dr. Karadzic asks: "Are the tits ours?"

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Sorry, what does he ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The English translation is: "Are the tits ours?" Referring to a feature. General Zivanovic responds: "They are. They're there for the first time" --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me, can you please stop for a second? Which line is this roughly in the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One-third of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: "Are the tits ours?"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Line 15, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Sorry, can you please give me some time to read the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the correct page in B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you to my colleague, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: By the way, just regarding the translation, the English word being "tits," that refers to when it says in the B/C/S - and apologies for my translation --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: You don't need to --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- it's the Tri Sise mountains.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: The what mountains -- oh, the [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Tri Sise, if I pronounce it correctly and I probably don't.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Actually we might need that translation because I did not understand your rendering of the Serbian language there. So I'd kindly request the translation. I've read this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go over to the next page in English, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, Dr. Karadzic, in this conversation with his military commander, General Zivanovic, is getting an earful of information and it's a very tactical discussion. They talk about elevations being reached, prisoners being taken, and Dr. Karadzic gives an order. He gives an order to attack. You would have seen in the second page, two-thirds of the way down, Dr. Karadzic tell General Zivanovic: "All right, General, full speed ahead. Tell Krstic order to go full steam." Now, you said earlier this morning, or earlier today, that as far as you knew, Dr. Karadzic wasn't involved in operational, tactical command over the army, and that's contradicted by this, and I called it an intercept, I apologise, this dictaphone tape recording, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, it's not. I didn't say that. Please don't put words into my mouth. I said by and large, or words that that effect, he did not -- he did not have a great interest in tactical operational matters. That's what I said. I think I was very clear earlier today. I think it can be checked in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What you said was: "In terms of operative and tactical levels of command over the army, I think you left that to the army itself."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: So I said "I think."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "I think you had responsibilities with regard to strategic decisions, but with regard to day-to-day operative and tactical levels, I don't think you were particularly involved."

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Precisely. He was not particularly involved. So what you said earlier on just now, that this document currently on display contradicts or contravenes my earlier statement, is simply untrue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It fits -- you're saying it fits, then, within the statement you've given that I just read back to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: It fits in within your imagination, perhaps, but it doesn't fit with my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll move on to another document, D2090. This is a document dated -- oh, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing B/C/S in English channel. I think it has been corrected. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I said the wrong 65 ter number, it's 2080.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And has your question about Sise been resolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think it's been ignored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It just referred to the three hilltops nearby Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Sise," I take it, was "tits" in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My mispronunciation, I'm told it's not a sh sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zametica, this is a document dated the next day, 9th of July, 1995, from General Krstic to the VRS --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, can we establish for sure whether that date, the date of the first document, was indeed the 8th or not? If we are going to continue claiming that this was on the next day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I said on or around the 8th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not have document -- I do not have date on that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not on that document, but I can -- tomorrow morning, I can direct Dr. Karadzic to the evidence regarding the date of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we continue, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So this is a document from General Krstic to the VRS Main Staff with an assessment of the situation in Srebrenica on the 9th of July --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: You mean 9th of -- I see two separate dates. I'm sorry to be interrupting you, but I see two separate -- 9th of July and 9th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: So I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There is nothing confusing about this document. This document is dated in the top left-hand corner, the 9th of July, 1995. And in the second paragraph, General Krstic relates the fierce attack that his units have carried out along the axes of Zeleni Jadar-Srebrenica-Pribojevici village and so forth, and indicates that they've created conditions for extending the attack toward Srebrenica. In paragraph 3, he --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica was referring to handwritten date on top right corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't ignore it for the moment. She may come back later on if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I wish to comment also on the translation of paragraph 2. It just goes to show that sometimes things can be lost in translation. In paragraph 2, there is no talk about a fierce attack. There is talk about "u snaznom naletu" which means a "strong push." It's not a fierce push but -- okay, it's a minor detail. I'm just drawing the attention of your fine self and the Tribunal that we have to be very careful regarding the language. I happened accidently to stumble against the Serbian version of the document, but please carry on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 3 sets out his decision for further actions, where he writes: "Taking advantage of the success achieved, regroup the forces and carry out a vigorous and decisive attack towards Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we scroll down to the bottom of the page, in both languages, please. Sorry, you'll have to go over to the second page in English for the date stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- sorry, I haven't even digested the first page. You're already pushing me on to the second page. I think this is slightly unfair.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Zametica. We can go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much. Just a quick comment on paragraph 1, he talks about the enemy firing all their available weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, I'll give you an opportunity to comment when I ask a question. I would just like to invite to you finish reading the document, as you'd requested.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if we can go over in English to the date stamp, we see that it's received on the 9th of July at 2330. If we can go back over to the English page -- the first page of the English. Pardon me, 2320. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zametica, General Krstic is sending this interim combat report exactly where he is supposed to, up to the VRS Main Staff. So I'd like us to go to another document --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Excuse me, when you say General Krstic is sending this report where it should be going to, the VRS Main Staff, and the Drina Corps, what exactly is the meaning of your words?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a lead-up to the next question --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Oh, I see, sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- in the next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: P2276, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The very same evening that you, in your written statement, have your conversation with Dr. Karadzic, General Tolimir issues an order which is copied to Dr. Karadzic for information and it's delivered to the Drina Corps command post, Generals Gvero and Krstic, personally. Now, it relates to the conduct of combat operations around Srebrenica, and it says, in paragraph 1, paragraph 2, paragraph 3, and paragraph 4, that the president of the republic has been informed of the combat operations, the president of the republic is satisfied with the results of the combat operations, he's ordered that follow-up combat operations take place, and in accordance with the order of the president --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please be more precise? Where does it say that I ordered it in -- as opposed to given my approval? Or consent? If the meaning is important, then let us take proper care of this meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have the document. So what -- please let us know when you have done the reading, Mr. Zametica. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I'm sorry, but I received a different interpretation than the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ignore the previous question. I think Mr. Zametica read the document. What is your question, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it is clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a minute. What is your question, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zametica, I want to go back again to your assertion that Dr. Karadzic wasn't involved in operational tactical command of the army, and here --

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: Can we -- can we just pause for a second? I mean, this is the second time I'm going to say this. I never said that. You say that I asserted that Dr. Karadzic was never involved in operation and tactical conduct of warfare. I never said anything of the kind and I repeat it now. It will be on the record. I repeat it now. He was largely uninterested. So I never asserted that he had not been involved in operational and tactical at any time whatsoever. I never said words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zametica, you've described the army as insubordinate. This is an example of General Krstic sending a report right up to where it's supposed to go, to the VRS Main Staff. If you look at this document, it's clear that the order we just looked at, D2 -- or the report we just looked at, D2080, went to Karadzic. 45 minutes later, and you can see by the time stamp on this document, the answer comes back from Dr. Karadzic. This is an example, Mr. Zametica, of the chain of command in the -- the chain of command working perfectly smoothly and contradicts your assertion that the army was out of control.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No. I think this is a very good example of how a clever lawyer like yourself puts two and two together and makes ten. And I shall elaborate on that. In this document currently on the monitor, you said Karadzic ordered this and that. In paragraph 1, in paragraph 2, you said, and in paragraph 3. In fact, if you actually bother to read the document, he doesn't order anything in paragraph 1. He simply informed. I shall read it: "The President of Republika Srpska has been informed of successful combat operations," blah, blah, blah. Second paragraph: "The president of the republic is satisfied ..." So being satisfied doesn't mean he's ordering anything. Being informed doesn't mean he's ordering anything. The only thing, in fact, he is ordering is to be found in paragraph 3, and I shall read it out for you: "The President of Republika Srpska ordered," repeat ordered, "that in the follow-up combat operations, full protection be ensured," repeat, full protection be ensured, "to UNPROFOR members and the Muslim civilian population and that they be guaranteed safety in the event of their crossover to the territory of Republika Srpska." And that's the only thing he ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you agree with me, then, the chain of command is working perfectly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ZAMETICA
utterances.text: No, I do not. I wish that were true, but it -- it unfortunately didn't work like that. Earlier today, I tried to make the point about the Army of Republika Srpska being basically a force unto itself. I don't know what better way of describing the state of affairs that existed at the time. The chain of command that you talk about did not really exist. It existed only when the Army of Republika Srpska, when it suited it to obey some order or instruction by Dr. Karadzic, then it did work. But otherwise, they did what they -- what they liked. They very much behaved like a force unto itself. So you're trying to establish the existence of a certain chain of command which was demonstrably not there. Only two -- three weeks, sorry, after this date, which is 9th of July here, the army is staging a silent coup d'état. What sort of chain of command are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to say. I've gone over time and I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zametica, have you ever testified before a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in a civil case regarding tenants once in Cambridge, many years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you're testifying here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
